title: A cache in spare memory
teaches: Caching in front of a database, hit-rate arithmetic, invalidation, and consistent hashing
summary: **A cache trades memory and staleness for speed and database load.** It answers repeated reads from memory and lets the database see only the misses.
**The database sees (1 − hit rate) of the reads.** Going from 90% hits to 99% cuts the database's load to a tenth, so measure the hit rate before anything else.
**memcached is a hash table in RAM, spread by the client.** Servers keep no disk copy, make no replicas and never talk to each other; the client hashes each key to choose a server.
**With cache-aside the application does the work.** It reads the cache, goes to the database on a miss, and fills the cache with what it found.
**Delete the cache entry on a write; don't set it.** Two writers setting the cache can finish in the wrong order and leave an old value there indefinitely; deletes agree in any order.
**A time to live bounds how stale an entry can be.** It costs misses on entries that had not changed, and catches the invalidations that went wrong.
**Placing keys by key mod n moves almost every key when n changes.** Going from 10 servers to 11 moves about 91% of keys, and every one of those is a miss.
**Consistent hashing moves only the keys that must move.** On a ring, adding an eleventh server moves about 1/11 of the keys, the ones on its arc.
**A cache becomes something the database depends on.** Once the database is sized for the misses, losing the cache sends it the full load.

blocks.text: By 2003 LiveJournal's databases were busy again, now with reads. Lesson 4's clusters had divided the writes, but the same popular journal entries, friends lists and user records were read thousands of times a second, and each read was a query on a database. Meanwhile the web servers, dozens of them, each had memory to spare: they needed processor time to build pages, not much RAM to hold them.

In May 2003 Brad Fitzpatrick wrote a program to put that spare memory to work. It ran on any machine with RAM to give and did one thing: store a value under a key and hand it back when asked. He called it **memcached**. It kept nothing on disk, made no copies, and its servers did not know about each other. If one restarted, whatever it held was gone, and the program reading from it went to the database instead, as it would have without the cache. Within a few years Facebook, Wikipedia, YouTube, Twitter and thousands of other sites ran it.[^memcached]

A **cache** is any store that keeps copies of data from a slower source so that repeated reads can be answered faster. The question this lesson keeps asking is how much a given cache actually saves, and what it costs in return. Both come down to one number, the hit rate, defined below.

On each server memcached is a **hash table** in memory. Each item holds a key of up to 250 bytes, a value of up to a megabyte, an expiry time and a few flags. When memory runs out, it throws away the item that has gone longest without being read; this is called evicting the **least recently used** (LRU) item, and it means the cache fills itself with whatever is read most without anyone deciding what that is.[^slabs] The client talks to it over TCP in lines of plain text: set a key with a value and a lifetime, get a key, delete a key.

blocks.caption: What memcached says on the wire and keeps in memory. A get that finds nothing answers END, and the application goes to the database.

blocks.text: The cluster has no leader and no shared state. The client library holds the list of servers and picks one for each key by hashing it, so the same key always goes to the same server. Lesson 1's ladder says why a cache on another machine is worth asking: a round trip inside the datacentre costs about half a millisecond, while a database query that touches disk costs several milliseconds, and one that has to queue behind others (lesson 2) costs more.

The usual way to use memcached is called **cache-aside**: the application asks the cache first. If the item is there, a **hit**, that is the answer. If not, a **miss**, the application queries the database, sends the reply on, and stores it in the cache for next time. The cache never talks to the database; the application does both halves.

The **hit rate**, the share of reads the cache answers, decides almost everything. With a hit rate h, the database sees (1 − h) of the reads. The average read takes h times the cache's time plus (1 − h) times the database's. Take 20,000 reads a second, a database that can answer 4,000, a cache read of 0.5 ms and a database read of 10 ms.

blocks.caption: Cache-aside at 20,000 reads a second in front of a database that can take 4,000 (the dots run at a two-hundredth of that, in slow motion). Blue dots are requests and green dots are answers: a request answered at the cache is a hit, and one that goes on to the database is a miss.
blocks.task: Guess how much the database's load falls from 90% hits to 99%, then raise the hit rate to 99%.

blocks.text: At 90% hits the database sees 2,000 reads a second, half its capacity, and the average read takes 1.45 ms. At 99% it sees 200, and the average is 0.6 ms. Going from 90 to 99 looks like a small improvement and is a tenfold cut in database load, because what matters is the misses, and they fell from ten in a hundred to one. At 80% the database gets 4,000 and is full. Small changes in the hit rate near the top move the database's load by large factors, which is why it is the first number to measure on any cache, and to keep measuring.

What sets the hit rate is how reads are spread over keys and how much memory the cache has. Reads on most sites are very uneven: a small share of items gets most of the reads. If the most-read 5% of items take 90% of the reads, a cache that holds those 5% has a 90% hit rate, and doubling its memory may add only a few points. To size a cache, log the keys read over a busy hour, sort them by how often each was read, and add up the sizes of the most-read keys until they cover the hit rate you want; that total, the **working set**, is the memory the cache needs. The arithmetic runs the other way too. Once a database is sized for the misses, it depends on the cache: if the hit rate falls from 99% to 90% because a cache server restarted empty, the database's load rises tenfold. Many reads missing at once and landing on the database together is a **miss storm**, and lesson 15 is about surviving one.

A cache holds copies, and copies go stale when the original changes. There are two ways to limit that. The first is a **time to live** (TTL): each item expires after, say, five minutes, and the next read refills it. An entry is never more than five minutes stale, at the cost of misses on items that had not changed. The second is **invalidation**: when the application writes to the database, it also removes or replaces the cache entry. Done right, readers see changes at once; done wrong, they see old data indefinitely. Most systems use both, invalidation for freshness and a TTL as a backstop for the invalidations that fail.[^karlton] Choose the TTL from how stale each kind of data may be: a user's display name can be an hour out of date, a count of items left in stock perhaps a few seconds. A TTL much shorter than the time between reads of a key turns every read into a miss.

The obvious invalidation is to update the cache with the new value on every write. That has a race. Two writers change the same row at about the same moment: A writes v1 to the database, then B writes v2. Each then sends its value to the cache. If A is held up between its two steps, by a pause in its runtime or a slow network, B's set arrives first and A's second. The database holds v2 and the cache holds v1, and nothing will correct it until the entry expires.

blocks.caption: Two writers update the same row, and writer A pauses briefly between updating the database and updating the cache. Time runs down the page.
blocks.task: Play it with set on write, then with delete on write.

blocks.text: Deleting the entry instead of setting it removes this race. Two deletes in either order leave the cache empty, and the next read fetches the current value from the database. The cost is one extra miss after every write. A narrower race remains, where a reader fetches an old value from the database just before a write and puts it in the cache just after the delete; Facebook met it at scale and solved it with leases, in lesson 15.

The first memcached clients chose a server the obvious way: hash the key to a number and take it modulo the number of servers. With ten servers, a key whose hash is 4,417 goes to server 7. It spreads keys evenly and costs nothing to compute. It also fails badly the day a server is added or removed. With eleven servers, 4,417 mod 11 is 6, and almost every key's server changes in the same way: going from 10 to 11 moves about ten keys in eleven, 91% of them. Each moved key is a miss on its new server, so adding cache capacity briefly takes the hit rate from 90% to about 8%: only the one key in eleven that stayed put can still hit. By the arithmetic of the hits and misses section, misses go from 10% of reads to 92%, about nine times the database's usual load.

In 1997 David Karger and colleagues at MIT published a way around this for web caches, which they called **consistent hashing**.[^karger] Hash the servers onto a circle as well as the keys, and give each key to the first server clockwise from it. Adding a server puts one new point on the circle, and only the keys between it and the server before it change hands, about one key in eleven when there are eleven. Removing a server hands its keys to the next one round and moves nothing else.

blocks.caption: Keys hashed onto a circle. With mod n they move to new servers almost wholesale; on a ring only the new server's arc changes hands.
blocks.task: Add a server with mod n, then switch to the ring and add one there.

blocks.text: One server at one point on the circle owns an uneven arc: some servers get twice their share of keys and some half. The fix is to put each server at many points round the circle, so the arcs average out; with a hundred or more points each, servers' shares come within roughly 10% of one another. Lesson 12 covers it with Amazon's Dynamo, which made it famous. Memcached clients took up consistent hashing in 2007, when Last.fm released a library called libketama that did exactly this, with each server at 160 points, and other client libraries copied it.

The trade a cache makes is now in numbers. It buys lower latency and a database a tenth or a hundredth as large. It costs memory, which is cheap when it is spare and not when it is bought for the purpose. It costs freshness: every design with a cache must say how stale a read may be, and for which reads. It costs code: with cache-aside every read path handles the miss and every write path handles invalidation. And it costs a dependency the database did not have, because a database sized for the misses cannot carry the full load.

Cache-aside is not the only arrangement. A **read-through** cache fetches from the database itself on a miss, so the application sees only the cache. A **write-through** cache takes writes and passes them on to the database, keeping itself current. Both move the miss and invalidation logic out of the application, and both make the cache part of the path that must not fail. Memcached chose the simplest arrangement, a cache that knows nothing about the database, and left the rest to the application, which is part of why it was easy to adopt everywhere.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Database load = (1 − hit rate) × reads; mean latency = h × cache + (1 − h) × database.
Delete on write, with a TTL behind it.
On a ring, adding the nth server moves about 1/n of the keys; with mod n almost all of them.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on caching
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A cache in front of a database answers 95% of 40,000 reads a second. How many reads a second reach the database?
items.why: The database sees the misses: (1 − 0.95) × 40,000 = 2,000. At 99% it would see 400.

items.ask: A team can raise its cache's hit rate from 90% to 99% by adding memory. What does that do to the database's read load?
choices: Cuts it by about a tenth, since 99 is about ten percent more than 90
Cuts it to a tenth, since misses fall from ten in a hundred to one
Leaves it almost the same, since most reads were hits already
items.why: The database's load is the miss rate times the reads. Misses fall from 10% to 1%, so the database sees a tenth as many reads.

items.ask: Why should a writer delete the cache entry after updating the database, rather than set it to the new value?
choices: Deleting is faster on the cache server than storing a new value of the same size, so writes return sooner
Two sets can land in the wrong order; two deletes cannot
A set can fail when memory is full, leaving the old value cached
items.why: If writer A sets v1 after writer B sets v2, the cache keeps v1 while the database holds v2. Two deletes leave the entry empty, and the next read fetches the current value.

items.ask: A memcached cluster places keys by hash mod n. It grows from 20 servers to 21 during the evening peak. What happens?
choices: About one key in twenty-one moves, so the hit rate dips by a few points
Nothing moves until each item's time to live runs out, so the change is spread over minutes
About twenty keys in twenty-one move to a new server, so nearly every read misses at once
items.why: With mod n almost every key's server changes when n does. Each moved key is a miss, and the database suddenly sees nearly the full read load. Consistent hashing would move about 1/21 of the keys.

items.ask: On a consistent-hashing ring with ten cache servers, one server fails. Which keys change server?
choices: Only the keys that were on the failed server, which pass to the next server clockwise
About half of all keys, since the remaining nine must even out the load between them
All keys, since every key's position on the ring is recomputed from the new count
items.why: Each key belongs to the first server clockwise from it. Removing one server's point changes the owner only of the keys on its arc.

items.ask: A database can take 3,000 reads a second. The site serves 50,000 reads a second through a cache with a 98% hit rate. A cache server restart drops the hit rate to 90% for a few minutes. What happens?
choices: The database's load goes from 1,000 to 5,000 reads a second, beyond what it can take
The database's load rises by about eight percent and stays within its capacity
Nothing at the database, because cache misses are answered from the other cache servers
items.why: At 98% the database sees 2% of 50,000, 1,000 a second. At 90% it sees 10%, 5,000 a second. A database sized for the misses depends on the hit rate staying high.

items.ask: Why did memcached keep no copy on disk and no replicas?
choices: Disks and networks of 2003 were too slow to keep up with the rate of writes to a cache
Everything in it could be rebuilt from the database, so losing a server cost misses, not data
Copies would have needed the servers to elect a leader, which no software of the time could do
items.why: The database stays the source of truth. A lost cache server costs a burst of misses, and leaving out durability and replication kept the program small, fast and easy to run.

memcached.title: Perl, then C
memcached.text: The first memcached was written in Perl and was soon rewritten in C for speed. Fitzpatrick's company Danga released it as free software, and its plain text protocol meant clients appeared quickly in every language a website was written in.

slabs.title: Slabs
slabs.text: To avoid the slow fragmentation that comes from allocating and freeing values of every size, memcached carves its memory into pages of fixed-size chunks (slabs), each class a little larger than the last, and stores each item in the smallest chunk that fits it. Each class keeps its own least-recently-used list.

karlton.title: Two hard things
karlton.text: A line often attributed to Phil Karlton, a programmer at Netscape, says there are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things. Programmers have been adding a third, off-by-one errors, ever since.

karger.title: From web caches to Akamai
karger.text: Karger's group was working on spreading web pages over many caches so that a popular page would not swamp any one of them. Two of the people involved, Tom Leighton and Danny Lewin, founded Akamai in 1998 on the idea, and it became the first large content delivery network (lesson 19).
